transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-04-11
Start time: 16:10 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Avery Cole (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dana Liu (Novus CTO), Marcus Grant (Lead ML Eng), Priya Sen (Infra), Evan Park (Product), Sara O'Neal (Security)

Summary:
Quick sandbox onramp for Redwood Hosted Chat/Text generation. Covered streaming behavior, key generation params (temp, max_tokens, top_p), retry/backoff patterns, idempotency hints, and console/Optimize tips for cost/latency. Touched on security (SOC2, KMS, VPC) and pilot next steps. Transcription imperfect in places; some words mis-attributed.

Topics covered:
- Streaming: chunking, partial updates, finalization events
- Params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, streaming vs sync differences
- Retries: exponential backoff, idempotency tokens, client-side vs server-side retry, circuit breakers
- Console/Optimize: batching suggestions, caching prefixes, quantization recommendations, cost estimates
- Security: SSO/SAML, SOC2, KMS/HSM, VPC peering for Private deployment

Action items (captured in metadata above, also spoken): send docs, schedule lab, run benchmark.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I see Dana, Marcus, Priya, Evan, Sara – thanks for the time. we'll keep this hands on and leave time for q's.
[00:12] Dana: yep thanks, we just want to get a sense of live streaming behavior and how retries work, our product has live chat and low latency limits, around 120–150ms p95 backend-to-client ideally.
[00:25] Samir: cool, that's a good target; quick note — p95 includes network, so we usually aim lower on the model side. we'll demo streaming and then show param knobs.
[00:38] Marcus: also curious about cost tradeoffs and whether we should use a smaller model fallback if traffic spikes.
[00:45] Avery: absolutely, we'll walk through model variants and the console Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization that can shave cost without big quality loss.
[00:53] Samir: starting demo — I'll trigger a streaming chat request from the sandbox. you'll see partial tokens arrive as delta events, then a final event. sometimes clients see interim punctuation or sentence fragments — that's expected.
[01:12] Samir: (typing noises) sending sample 2-turn convo now. note, we set temperature 0.6 and top_p 0.9.
[01:21] Speaker 6: [inaudible]
[01:28] Samir: partial chunk... "The recommended approach is to buffer short fragments until you hit the sentence boundary or a time threshold (we recommend ~200ms)" — buffer heuristics vary per client.
[01:43] Priya: quick question — is the partial chunk re-sent on retry or do we re-play from start?
[01:50] Samir: good call; server may resume from last committed KV cache if using conversation_id + cache. but for stateless streaming you should use idempotency tokens and replay from last confirmed token boundary. in practice we support resume on the same request if you have the session and kv cache pinned on the routing layer.
[02:12] Marcus: kv cache— you mean the key-value cache for past tokens? is that sticky per GPU? I'm thinking about multi-AZ routing.
[02:21] Samir: yes, kv cache is per model instance and can be sharded; Redwood routing will pin sessions by policy (latency, region) and optionally fall back to a compatible variant; multi-AZ increases durability but may add cross-AZ latency if we have to fetch cache.
[02:36] Dana: what about retries — we want automatic client retries but avoid duplicate outputs.
[02:41] Avery: recommended: 1) use idempotency tokens on request start 2) exponential backoff with jitter on 5xx and 429 3) client-side dedupe on same token id. also, we return a request_id to help correlate logs in the Console.
[02:57] Evan: what's the typical backoff schedule? 200ms initial?
[03:01] Samir: common is 200–500ms base, * 2 each attempt, cap around 5–10s; and abort after 3 attempts for interactive flows. for batch jobs you'll tolerate longer windows.
[03:15] Sara: security question — if we're using Hosted but need KMS for encrypting training/prompt logs, what's supported?
[03:23] Avery: we support bring-your-own KMS in Dedicated and Private; for Hosted we have a managed KMS but we can integrate customer KMS for Private deployments; we'll send the SOC2 brief and KMS integration doc.
[03:35] Samir: coming back to streaming: another hack is to send shorter max_tokens on first pass to reduce tail latency and request follow-up completions if needed; this helps with responsiveness on mobile.
[03:50] Marcus: won't that break context?
[03:53] Samir: small tradeoff — if you do prefix caching and maintain conversation state, incremental completions compose fine. the console shows token cost per route so you can measure overhead.
[04:05] [05:00] Samir: demo note — sometimes transcripts show punctuation weirdly in the SDK logs; we put markers in the stream: 'delta' events, 'choice' events, final 'done' event. client libraries wrap that for you.
[05:28] Marcus: any pointers on concurrency limits and bursting? we expect surges from product launches.
[05:35] Avery: Dedicated has predictable throughput and burst capacity; for Hosted we recommend increasing concurrency pool in the client and using smart routing to fallback to cheaper model variants during peaks; Optimize can suggest autoscale settings after it sees your workload.
[05:52] Priya: about fallbacks — how graceful is quality degradation? do you get abrupt jarring answers?
[05:58] Samir: we prefer staged rollbacks: canary to smaller variant, we also recommend prompt engineering to degrade gracefully—structured responses or adding system prompts to indicate low-confidence. Redwood console lets you define fallback policies per route.
[06:15] Dana: ok, on the retry front if a stream fails halfway and client reconnects, are tokens double-charged?
[06:22] Avery: billing is based on tokens committed to the final model output; transient partial fragments aren't charged unless the model completes them. but if you re-send and the model produces the same content twice, you'll be billed for both completions. that's why idempotency + resume is important.
[06:38] Marcus: can we test with our dev payloads — we'll want to benchmark latency for our average turn length (350 tokens) under 95th percentile.
[06:46] Avery: yes, pilot recommended — we can run a 10k token/day bench as a spike test; Samir will share the checklist.
[06:54] Samir: also note parameters: temperature controls randomness; for deterministic assistant style keep 0.0–0.2; for creative use 0.6+. top_p is alternative nucleus sampling; they can interact. lowering both reduces variance and typically reduces token churn.
[07:16] Evan: what about stop sequences? we have structured responses, how reliable are they with streaming?
[07:22] Samir: stop sequences are honored at generation time; streaming may produce the bits before the stop boundary but final event will show termination. client should trim trailing partials to the last stop token. small corner case with tokenization mismatch can show trailing punctuation; we'll show a snippet.
[07:41] Samir: (shares code) here's a curl example and Node snippet; for streaming we use chunked transfer encoding SSE or websockets; SDK wraps and emits 'data' events.
[08:00] Marcus: are there SDKs for our stack? we use Go and Typescript.
[08:05] Avery: yes officially supported TS/Node and Python; Go has community libs and we can provide example wrappers — Samir will attach sample Go client.
[08:16] Priya: how do you recommend handling rate limits—should we token-bucket client-side?
[08:21] Samir: yes, token-bucket + circuit breaker. also use the console rate metrics to tune the bucket. on retries prefer increasing backoff rather than more aggressive bursts.
[08:36] Dana: if we want to encrypt logs to our KMS keys, how will that work with Hosted?
[08:42] Avery: Hosted keeps customer data encrypted at rest; for strict KMS control we recommend Redwood Private or Dedicated with BYOK. Hosted can provide long-term retention settings and delete-on-request policies. we'll send the specifics.
[08:58] [09:30] Samir: switching topics: Optimize tips — automatic batching rules, prefix cache recommendations, quantization levels. For example, for a diagnostic workload with many short prompts, batching 8–16 requests can reduce per-token latency and cost by up to 20%.
[09:54] Marcus: quantization—does that affect quality on instruction-following models?
[09:59] Samir: small impact depending on quant level; Optimize will suggest q4_0 or q5 variants and run local quality checks vs your eval set. it's model-dependent.
[10:10] Evan: console — can we preview per-route cost and token breakdown?
[10:14] Avery: yes Console shows token-level cost, latency histograms, and per-token cost delta when you change model or quant. we can walk the Console in the lab.
[10:28] Samir: small gotcha — streaming with extremely low timeouts can lead to partial chunks being cut; prefer client timeout > retry schedule to give the model time to respond.
[10:40] Priya: what about idempotency token format?
[10:44] Samir: any UUID-like string is fine; include session metadata server side for dedupe.
[10:50] Dana: okay, this is good. what's the recommended pilot scope?
[10:55] Avery: 2-week pilot, run 1k–10k token/day tests with real payloads, measure p50/p95, tune batching + quant + fallback policies, then decide on Dedicated vs Hosted.
[11:08] Marcus: timeline — we'll sync engineering priorities and get back to you.
[11:11] Avery: next steps recap: I send notebook + creds + pricing, Samir sends benchmark checklist and code snippets, Marcus/ Priya confirm KV/peering questions and SLO. schedule hands-on lab next Tue (Avery to propose times).
[11:30] Evan: small Q: are there webhooks for async completions?
[11:34] Samir: yes, you can do async jobs and webhook callbacks; we also support long-poll and job endpoints for batch flows.
[11:42] Sara: compliance: can you provide logging redaction options?
[11:46] Avery: yes we support PII redaction hooks, audit logs, and data retention policies — we will attach the security appendix.
[12:00] [12:10] Dana: great, thanks everyone. appreciate the concise demo.
[12:15] Avery: thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed times.

End of transcript.
